a.summary: The deprecated `sign(SequencedCollection)` is abstract and is the only implementation hook for positional signing, so third-party implementors are forced to implement a `forRemoval` method and the deprecation cannot be honoured without a second breaking change that MIGRATION.md promises will not happen.
a.failure_scenario: A third-party class `implements Transaction` must supply `sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>)` because it is abstract. There is no non-deprecated method it can implement instead: `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` (Transaction.java:845) is a `default` that calls `sign(signers)`, and all five other `signInOrder*` defaults (lines 850, 855, 860, 865, 870) likewise delegate to deprecated members. So an implementor recompiling against this release gets an unavoidable deprecation warning (JLS 9.6.4.6 makes overriding a use), with no migration available. When the removal actually happens, `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` has nothing left to delegate to and must become abstract — which breaks source and binary compatibility for every third-party `Transaction`, directly contradicting MIGRATION.md:106-107 ("New instance methods have defaults, so existing `Transaction` implementations do not need additional method overrides"). The deprecation as written is therefore not executable as an additive change, which is exactly what AGENTS.md's published-library rule is meant to prevent.

b.summary: Five of the six new `signInOrder*` instance defaults route through the deprecated `sign*` chain instead of through `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)`, so an override of the new positional name is honoured by only one of its six entry points — the opposite of the `signByKey` family, where all six funnel through `signByKey(Collection)`.
b.failure_scenario: A consumer implementing `Transaction` migrates off the `forRemoval` name by overriding the new one: `@Override public void signInOrder(SequencedCollection<Signer> signers) { audit(signers); super.signInOrder(signers); }`. `tx.signInOrder(signers)` runs the audit. `tx.signInOrder(blockHash, signers)` does not — it calls `sign(recentBlockHash, signers)` (Transaction.java:856), which calls `setRecentBlockHash` then the abstract `sign(signers)`, never touching the override. Same for `signInOrder(base58Hash, signers)`, `signInOrderAndBase64Encode(signers)`, and both blockhash Base64 variants: the transaction is signed with the audit hook silently skipped. The equivalent `signByKey` override is honoured by all six of its entry points (Transaction.java:889, 896, 902, 907, 913 all call `signByKey(...)` virtually). A second consequence: because every `signInOrder*` default body is written purely in terms of members marked `forRemoval`, none of them has a body that survives removal, so MIGRATION.md:106-107's "New instance methods have defaults, so existing `Transaction` implementations do not need additional method overrides" stops being true the moment the deprecated members go.

instructions.question: How does the defect described by `b` relate to the defect described by `a`?
instructions.focus: Compare the defects, not the wording. Two findings about the same code can still be different defects.

criteria: Different defects: fixing the defect `a` describes would leave the defect `b` describes unfixed, even when both sit in the same code.
The same underlying defect, but `b` narrows it, re-scopes which instances or inputs it covers, or reports it at a different place. Not a different defect in adjacent code.
The same defect restated in different words: fixing one fixes the other.

claims_new_evidence.instructions: Does `b` cite evidence that `a` does not?

criteria.true: `b` names a file, test, command, observation, or reproduction that `a` does not mention.
criteria.false: `b` cites nothing beyond what `a` already cites, or cites nothing at all.
